chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Fadalah, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu 'Abdillah عليه السلام, who said:

Dawud ibn 'Ali asked me about a man who used to come to another man's house, and he forbade him from coming to his house, but he refused to comply. So he went to the ruler, and the ruler said, 'If he does it, then kill him.'

He said: 'So he killed him. What do you think about it?' I said: 'I hold that he should not kill him. If this were upheld, then any person could wish to say of his enemy: he entered my house, so I killed him.'

key_terms.بَيْتَ رَجُلٍ: another man's house; the protected private space at issue
key_terms.رَجُلٍ: a man; the legal subject in the case
key_terms.فَاقْتُلْهُ: kill him; the order under discussion in the case
key_terms.لِعَدُوِّهِ: his enemy; indicating the danger of fabricated claims against opponents

ai.seo_question: Can someone lawfully kill a person for entering his house after being warned not to come?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling that a person is not permitted to kill someone merely for repeatedly entering his house after being forbidden, even if a ruler had said so in that specific case. The Imam عليه السلام rejects such a precedent because it would open the door to false claims and abuse against enemies, showing concern for due restraint in cases involving bloodshed.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications:
Hadith.5395 - Al-Husayn ibn Said narrated from Fadalah from Dawud ibn Farqad from Abu Abdullah (as), that Imam (as) recounted:
"Dawud ibn Ali asked me about a man who used to visit another man's house, and the owner forbade him from coming to his house, but he refused to stop. So the owner went to the ruler, and the ruler said: 'If he does it again, kill him.'
So the man killed him. What is your opinion on this?"
So I (Imam (as)) said: "I see that he should not have killed him. If this ruling were upheld, then anyone could later claim that an enemy entered their house, and they killed him."
